schools.summary: Gregory reads the naming of Uz — a land of the Gentiles — as praise: it is highest testimony to be good among the wicked, as Lot was, and as Job the brother to dragons was.
Gill traces Uz to the son of Nahor (or of Seir in Edom) and locates Job in Arabia Deserta near the Sabeans, Chaldeans, and Edom.

Ellicott counts three men named Uz and places Job's home south of Palestine toward Edom, glossing 'perfect' by Noah and Christ's standard; Keil and Delitzsch frame the book's whole question — why afflictions befall the righteous.
Clarke, with Mr. Good, makes all the persons Edomite Arabs of Idumea and argues Job lived after the Law (Moses the likely author); Wesley calls Uz part of Arabia and 'perfect' sincere, not legal.
Henry gives the fourfold portrait — feared God, perfect yet not sinless (Job 9:20), upright, eschewing evil — and marvels Job was good in so bad a place.

debates.question: When did Job live, and who wrote the book?

sides.position: in the patriarchal age, soon after or before Abraham; the most ancient book, likely written by Job himself
after the giving of the Law, from its echoes of the Mosaic institutions; Moses the likely author

themes: a man in the land of Uz
the date and author of Job

schools.summary: Gill notes the children were born to Job by his wife in lawful wedlock — she still living and to reappear.
Henry makes the count an emblem of prosperity: children a heritage of the Lord (Ps. 127:3), a blessing to good parents.
Keil and Delitzsch survey the large, princely household — numbers large but not invented, wealth measured by flocks; Ellicott catches the symmetry with the like number restored at Job 42:13.

themes: children a heritage of the Lord

schools.summary: Gill notes the sheep named first as the largest and most useful part, needing a large pasturage.
Henry: riches 'substance' by common speech though shadows to the soul (Prov. 23:5); wealth reckoned by cattle and dominion over the creatures (Ps. 8:6).
Clarke gives the Targum's division of the estate and calls Job the chief emir; Wesley notes the camels' usefulness and the valued she-asses.
Keil and Delitzsch make Job the greatest of the sons of the east from Arabia Deserta; Ellicott calls 'men of the east' indefinite and notes the Arabs still name the region the land of Job.

themes: greatest of the men of the east

schools.summary: Gill reads the feasts as innocent gatherings by turns to cherish love, perhaps at sheep-shearing, in private homes not public houses.
Henry dwells on a father's comfort in children settled, thriving, healthy, and living in unity; Job stays away like Barzillai (2 Sam. 19:35), granting youthful liberty.
Clarke takes 'his day' as a birthday festival; Wesley allows the birthday or the month's first day, and calls the feasting a testimony of brotherly love.
Ellicott reads 'every one his day' as probably his birthday, comparing Gen. 40:20 and Mark 6:21.

debates.question: What does 'every one his day' mean?

sides.position: a birthday festival kept in turn
an appointed day in a settled rotation, not necessarily a birthday

schools.summary: Henry reads a godly jealousy: fearing profane thoughts in their mirth, Job sanctifies his children, rises early, and offers a sacrifice for each, continually (John 13:10).
Gill takes the sanctifying at the end of each rotation of feasts.
Keil and Delitzsch note the verbs describe a habitually repeated act; Ellicott sees the father acting as priest, a mark that Job stood outside the Mosaic law, like the patriarchs.
Wesley reads 'cursed' as despising or slighting God, not gross cursing; Clarke weighs 'blessed the gods' (idolatry) or Mr. Good's 'nor blessed God,' owning the plain sense the readier.

debates.question: What does 'cursed God in their hearts' mean?

sides.position: cursed, despised, or slighted God — the plain received sense
literally 'blessed,' a euphemism, or a bidding-farewell to and dismissing of God
possibly 'blessed the gods' (idolatry), or with Mr. Good 'nor blessed God'

themes: Job as priest of his household
it may be my sons have sinned

schools.summary: Gregory frames Scripture as a mirror showing both the saints' excellencies and their falls — Job made greater by temptation, David brought to the ground.
Gill takes the 'sons of God' for the angels, so called by creation, likeness, and obedience, who present themselves and go forth.
Henry allows either a meeting of saints on earth (Gen. 6:2) or angels in heaven, into which Satan intrudes, and reads the whole as parabolical like Micaiah (1 Kings 22:19).

Wesley reads a parabolical representation that God governs all actions of men and devils; Clarke, with Peters, calls it the prophetic way of representing a real transaction founded on the truth of good and bad angels, and warns against denying the devil's existence (1 Pet. 5:8).
Ellicott takes the 'sons of God' probably as angels, or an unseen-world incident parallel to earthly worship.

sides.position: the angels, the host of heaven
possibly an assembly of worshippers (saints) on earth

debates.question: Is the heavenly council literal or figurative?

sides.position: a parabolical representation, like Micaiah's vision
a real transaction of the unseen world, prophetically represented

outliers.note: Turns the passage into a polemic against those who deny the devil's existence — a denial he calls one of the very 'depths of Satan,' since the unwatchful become his easy prey.

themes: the sons of God present themselves

schools.summary: Gill: the omniscient God asks not to learn but to chide the intruder and draw out what he had marked, leading on to Job.

Keil and Delitzsch parse the present 'whence comest thou' and the two verbs of restless roaming, with Peter's 'peripatetic' echo and the Arabs' name for the devil; Ellicott notes Peter had the passage in mind (1 Pet. 5:8).
Clarke surveys the old versions, takes 'earth' as 'that land,' and finds in the intensive verb the devil's earnest, determined pursuit of men's ruin.

themes: going to and fro in the earth

schools.summary: Gill renders 'hast thou set thy heart upon Job' — Satan longing to have him as he desired Peter — and hears sarcasm and God's indignation.
Keil and Delitzsch mark the 'for' giving the ground, and the skilful repetition of Job's four predicates now in the LORD's own mouth.
Clarke: hast thou placed thy heart on Job, viewed his conduct while seeking whom to devour?
Henry finds God's commendation designed to aggravate Satan's apostasy, answer his boast, and anticipate his accusation — we have an advocate before we are accused.

themes: hast thou considered my servant Job
none like him in the earth

schools.summary: Gill marks how much the sly query concedes — no sin charged, the fear of God owned — while insinuating a mercenary religion by the slanderer's way of the question.

Keil and Delitzsch set the charge in the accuser's day-and-night role (Rev. 12:10), denying that true piety can exist; Ellicott calls it a disbelief in human goodness and names the book's object — man victorious over Satan.
Henry weighs the half-truth: Job did not fear God for nought, yet would have without it; to look to the eternal recompense is not mercenary, but to aim at temporal gain is spiritual idolatry.

themes: doth Job fear God for nought

schools.summary: Gill expounds the hedge as a wall of protection on every side — love, power, providence, angels, God a wall of fire — which Satan grudgingly makes the sole cause of Job's fear.
Clarke: God fortified Job as with spikes and spears, the object of peculiar care, not exposed to common trials.
Henry gives the double picture — God protected and prospered Job; the blessing of the LORD makes rich, which Satan himself owns while speaking with vexation.
Keil and Delitzsch: the permission is at once a command, for God is creator even of calamity (Isa. 45:7); yet the affliction has no ground in any sin of Job's.
Gill: Satan asks God to withdraw the hand of providence and strike 'now,' rejecting a slight trial for 'all that he hath,' knowing Job's integrity.
Clarke reads the wager as the cynic's creed that every man has his price, and turns it back — God has multitudes who will trust him though he slay them, as Job did.
Henry marks the devil's slight and spiteful speech, the 'curse' that is really 'bless' (cf. Naboth, 1 Kings 21:10), and the vast stake — Satan's empire over mankind if Job fall.

themes: the stake of the whole book

schools.summary: Gill: the permission is given not from displeasure but to confound Satan and try Job's grace; God alone disposes, Satan has only what is given.
Clarke notes Satan cannot take even an ass but by God's permission, his malice bounded; Wesley owns it strange yet done for God's glory, Job's honour, and his people's encouragement.
Ellicott makes it Scripture's settled teaching that evil is held in check by One who directs it to his ends (2 Cor. 12:7).
Henry joins the wonder (the turtle-dove given to the adversary, as Peter was sifted, Luke 22:31) and the comfort (God has the devil in a chain, Rev. 20:1); the body reserved, the estate exposed.

themes: all that he hath is in thy power

schools.summary: Gill cannot fix the day, doubting it was the morrow of Satan's leave, since it took time to bring the Sabeans and Chaldeans to march.
Keil and Delitzsch note the blow fell on the very day Job had held morning worship and knew his children gathered at the eldest son's house.
Henry makes the timing deliberate cruelty — Satan struck at the hour of richest feasting and fullest repose, that the calamity might be the more grievous (Isa. 21:4).
Clarke reports the Targum's 'first day of the week' and takes it for one of the birthday festivals.
Gill corrects the old fancy that the messenger was an evil spirit — he was one of Job's own servants, escaped from the calamity.
Keil and Delitzsch set the scene of ordinary industry — the oxen ploughing, the asses feeding — that the disaster interrupts.
Clarke notes the she-asses as the domesticated, valued kind; Wesley marks Satan's ordering that the messengers follow at once, so Job have no leisure to recollect himself.
Henry: the loss came in the way of duty (the oxen ploughing under the servant's eye), and the single survivor was spared only that Job might have certain intelligence by an eye-witness.

themes: the oxen and asses at work
I only am escaped to tell thee

schools.summary: Gill reads 'Sheba fell,' a host of Sabeans descended from Sheba son of Jokshan (Abraham by Keturah), dwelling in barren Arabia Deserta, Job's near neighbours.

Clarke notes the Vulgate's 'people' against the LXX/Syriac/Arabic 'marauding party' and the Chaldee's Lilith, reconciling them as banditti of Keturah's line; Wesley calls them a wandering people who lived by robbery.
Ellicott weighs the three Shebas of Genesis and judges it the grandson of Abraham through Jokshan, a predatory people bordering on Job (Ezek. 38:13).

debates.question: Are 'the Sabeans' a settled people or a marauding band?

sides.position: a settled people or tribe (the Vulgate's reading), descendants of Sheba son of Jokshan, near neighbours of Job
a predatory marauding party (LXX, Syriac, Arabic), the Chaldee even naming Lilith queen of Zamargad

themes: I only am escaped to tell thee

schools.summary: Gill marks the merciless speed — the second messenger before the first is done — Satan allowing no breathing-time for prayer or meditation.
Clarke takes the 'fire of God' for lightning, the prince of the air directing it; Wesley hears its suggestion that God seemed angry at Job's very offerings.
Ellicott agrees it can hardly be other than lightning (Gen. 19:24; 2 Kings 1:10), the OT seeing nature's convulsions as God's immediate act, though here a divine revelation.
Henry: the sheep of Job's sacrifices were taken as if God punished him in his own service — Satan misrepresenting God as a hard Master to tempt Job to think it vain to serve him.

themes: God made to seem the enemy

schools.summary: Gill notes the third messenger arrived before the last had finished.
Clarke traces the Chaldeans (Casdim) to Chesed son of Nahor, living on rapine and dividing into three bands for the camels; Wesley adds they lived upon spoil (Xenophon).
Ellicott derives them from Chesed (Gen. 22:22), noting the blow from the opposite quarter; Keil and Delitzsch defend the early Semitic and Nahor-Chaldeans of patriarchal times against a late dating.

debates.question: Does the mention of the Chaldeans point to a late date for the book?

sides.position: the Chaldeans as marauders point to a seventh-century (or Uzziah-era) composition
holders: Ewald (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Renan (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: early Semitic and Nahor-Chaldeans existed from patriarchal times; the mention proves nothing late

schools.summary: Gill notes the fourth messenger was a servant in attendance at the children's feast.

Keil and Delitzsch parse the particle of continuity, the epicene term for the young people, and the wind from the desert's farthest end — in one day Job bereft of all Jehovah's gifts; Ellicott reads the marvellous accumulation as the distinct, supernatural work of Satan by the permission of v.12.

themes: the worst blow kept for last

schools.summary: Gill notes the strong, extraordinary wind from the Arabian wilderness, prefaced by a 'behold' to rouse wonder.

Clarke sees the prince of the air directing four currents against the four corners; Wesley (with Henry) marks the greatest loss reserved for last, the children taken when Job most needed them — miserable comforters all creatures.
Keil and Delitzsch mark the turning-point: heard sitting through the first three, at his children's death Job rises, yet humbling himself under God's hand.
Henry: the children died together, suddenly, feasting not praying, by a devil's wind (Eph. 2:2) that looked like God's hand — as Bildad would later construe it (Job 8:4).

themes: the great wind from the wilderness
the four corners of the house
the devil's wind that seemed God's hand
all is taken in one day

schools.summary: Gill lingers on 'then': Job heard the loss of substance sedately, but at his children's death arose, deeply moved yet composed in body and mind.

Henry reads a man both feeling and faithful — rending and shaving as real sorrow without indecent passion, then falling in penitent submission (hypocrites cry not, Job 36:13); some think he rent his clothes at Satan's blasphemous suggestions.
Clarke lists the ancient signs of grief and Job's prostration; Wesley marks the wonder — instead of cursing, Job adored God's sovereignty, justice, and goodness.
Ellicott sets Job's worship beside David (2 Sam. 12:20) and Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:1), sorrow forcing us into God's presence; Keil and Delitzsch: not despair but humbling under the mighty hand.

themes: Job arose and rent his mantle
worship where a curse was foretold

schools.summary: Gill takes the nakedness literally of the body at birth and death — we bring nothing in (1 Tim. 6:7), which may look back to this saying.
Henry unfolds the quieting thoughts: Job but where he began and where he must end, looking past the Sabeans and Chaldeans to the first Cause who gave and took.
Clarke reads 'thither' as the ground, not the womb, and records the Chaldee's 'the Word of the LORD gave'; Wesley reads the womb as our common mother the earth (Gen. 3:19).
Ellicott notes 'blessed be the name' is the very word Satan used contrarily in v.11, so Satan was first foiled; Keil and Delitzsch set the confession as Job's humbling under God's hand.

debates.question: What does 'naked shall I return thither' mean?

sides.position: back to the mother's womb, taken figuratively for our common mother the earth (cf. Gen. 3:19)
not the womb but the ground on which he was falling — 'there'

themes: the LORD gave and hath taken away
Satan foiled for the first time

schools.summary: Gill: not that Job was sinless, but that in all he did and said there was nothing unbecoming, and nothing of the curse Satan foretold.

Clarke makes this the transaction that coloured Job's character, Satan utterly disappointed, and ties Job's continual offerings to the Mosaic law (Lev. 9:7); Wesley reads 'not imputed folly to God' — Job harboured no dishonourable thought.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh 'uttered nothing absurd' (Jerome) against 'attributed no folly to God,' siding for the latter; Ellicott glosses 'foolishly' as reproach or guilt (cf. Job 6:6), just after Satan's first defeat.
Henry: the Holy Ghost's testimony to Job's constancy — he did not attribute folly to God, for discontent charges God with folly, and against it Job watched.

debates.question: What does 'nor charged God foolishly' mean?

sides.position: he uttered nothing absurd or unseemly against God
holders: Jerome (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: he did not attribute folly to God

outliers.note: Hint that the verdict covers only 'all this' thus far — the writer intimates that later on Job would commit himself with some unwise thoughts of God's government.

themes: in all this Job sinned not
the meaning of the disputed phrase
